newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's elephants get birth control shots.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's elephants get birth control shots.

text.p: South Africa's elephants are being put on birth control pills in a bid to find an alternative to the annual bloody cull in which hundreds are killed.
The cull evokes outrage from animal lovers but the parks board says elephant over-population leads to destruction of vegetation to the detriment of other animals in the park.
The South African National Parks Board said in a statement on Wednesday that the experimental programme, a world first, was being carried out by local and U.S. scientists in the Kruger National Park.
"Wildlife biologists just completed identifying and administering the vaccine to 21 female adult elephants," it said.

"They will return next month to administer a second dose. The vaccine is not known to influence elephant behaviour and does not contain hormones or steroids. This project is the first to administer the vaccine to wild elephants."
The vaccine, which was developed in the United States and has been successfully tested on wild deer and horses there, blocks fertilisation by preventing sperm from attaching to eggs.
Robbie Robinson, chief executive of the parks board, said the programme could be of tremendous benefit.
"This research is in total agreement with our undertaking to explore all alternatives to killing in our research to find a better way of managing our elephant population," he said.
The Kruger Park, a game reserve about the size of Israel, has between 7,500 and 8,000 elephants which the parks board regards as the maximum number it can hold.
Every year, with the exception of this year, about 600 of the animals have been shot with paralysing drugs from helicopters and then killed as they lie on the ground.

In recent years the board has tried to combat over- population by tranquillising entire family groups of elephants and moving them to private game reserves, but these reserves also have limited capacity.
The contraception programme is being sponsored by the Humane Society of the United States, whose president Paul Irwin said:
"South Africa has shown the world that people once divided can live together in harmony. They can also be an example of a nation that peacefully co-exists with wildlife populations."
Elephant numbers in Africa as a whole were cut by half to 600,000 in the 10 years to 1989, mainly because of ivory poachers. An international ban on ivory trade has since been implemented.
Southern African states have opposed the ban, saying the sale of ivory from healthy elephant populations could help to finance wildlife conservation.
